US skips UN human rights review, drawing criticism

The meeting was postponed until January after Washington refused to take part, saying participation would imply support for the UN Human Rights Council.

The empty seat of the US delegation, during the 60th session of the Human Rights Council, at the European headquarters of the United Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, Sep 8, 2025. (Photo: AP/Salvatore Di Nolfi)

GENEVA: The Un ited States spurned a UN meeting on Tuesday (Nov 10) where its human rights record un der US President Donald Trump was due to be examined, drawing criticism from rights groups who say violations have surged to levels not seen in decades. Washington disengaged from the Geneva-based UN Human Rights Co un cil last year, citing an anti-Israel bias, and this is the second year in a row that it has skipped its own review - a process that even authoritarian state s take part in. The US left its seat on the stage of the UN meeting empty and the council decided to postpone the event until January. A US State Department spokesperson said participation would imply endorsement of the co un cil's work.

"This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it p us hes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, without responding to allegations about the US record. The 47-member co un cil has not directly criticised Washington's rights record but its appointed experts have, such as over migrant deportations. Washington said deportations wer e carried out in accordance with US immigration law.

QUESTIONS ON ABORTION AND DEATH PENALTY The Un iversal Periodic Review asks all 193 UN member states to submit a rights report every few years and these are review ed by other states , which provide non-binding recommendations. UN documents show co un tries had planned on Tuesday to raise issues such as abortion and the death penalty. US and international non-governmental organisations also sent nearly 200 UN submissions covering topics from migration to racial discrimination. “We've seen attacks on f un damental human rights and civil liberties un precedented in generations," Jamil Dakwar , of the American Civil Liberties Un ion , told reporters in Geneva. "Enough is enough." Fourteen co un tries are due to take part in the review process in Geneva this month. In Trump's first term in office, the US submitted its UPR report. Noor Abdalla, wife of pro-Palestinian student activist Mahmoud Khalil, who was held in immigration detention last year, is among campaigners pressing UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk to promptly hold a briefing on the US rights situation, even in Washington's absence. "When the most powerful government in the world is not held acco un table, they think that they can do whatever they want," Abdalla told reporters. However, diplomats were sceptical given that few states want to confront Washington. "The view is to leave the door open and hope they come back in two years," said a diplomat.

Defiant Hegseth blasts impeachment effort ahead of House vote

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth also thanked US President Donald Trump for his support as lawmakers prepared to vote on eight articles of impeachment against him.

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth holds a press briefing at the Pentagon in Washington, DC, US, November 10, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

WASHINGTON: Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday (Nov 10) blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce that would embolden US adversaries, as he lashed out at his political opponents in Congress and the media in an unapologetic defence of his record. Striking a defiant tone at a Pentagon news briefing, Hegseth thanked US President Donald Trump for his continued support as the House of Representatives scheduled a procedural vote for late Tuesday that will test support for his impeachment. Hegseth said past impeachments of Trump had ultimately failed, and added: "Both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House. Now they're trying a third time. This time against a member of his cabinet."

US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment against H egseth on Monday. Massie said in a post on X that if the House of Representatives can overcome Tuesday's procedural effort, "we will proceed to a real debate and vote on the Articles of Impeachment." Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with Trump’s Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on Jan 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats. Hegseth is accused of various abuses of power in office, including issuing orders to go to war with Iran without an imminent threat or approval from Congress. Voter anger over the Iran war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections . A new Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end the war with Iran.

US Representative Thomas Massie (R-KY) holds a press conference about his resolution to impeach Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, US, Nov 9, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein)

Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war. Hegseth declined to be drawn into responding to Vance, but defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran's military has been left in ruins. "History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now," he said. Hegseth cited US Secretary of State Marco Rubio as saying of the war: "It's not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary, and that's certainly how I feel. It was a necessary undertaking." Trump repeated his backing of Hegseth in a post on his Truth Social platform just after the Pentagon briefing ended. "Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!" he wrote. A polarizing figure in American politics, Hegseth would be the first US defense secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title "secretary of war." Hegseth, a former Fox News host, calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. But even some Republicans say his strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the administration seeks a US$1.5 trillion defense spending package. In a possible nod to the spending requests, Hegseth said Republicans should use their final weeks in control of Congress to deliver wins for the American people instead of pursuing his impeachment. If he's still around next year, Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, including his firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other top military officers.

What we know about Megaspeed, Singapore-based customer of Nvidia

The US is looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who is an alleged spy and a former executive at Megaspeed.

SINGAPORE: Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed faces renewed scrutiny as the United States looks into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , alleged to be a spy for Beijing . Here are details of Megaspeed, where Huang used to be an executive. WHAT IS MEGASPEED? Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International before changing its name to Megaspeed International in March 2023, its business filings showed. It is wholly owned by Singapore-registered Swiftdata incorporated in October 2023, which says providing hosting services by non-data centres is its principal activity.

Two Singapore citizens are listed as officers of both companies. Tan Yong Pong was appointed a director of Swiftdata on Oct 31, 2023, before becoming a director of Megaspeed less than two weeks later. The same month, Huang Le ended an eight-month tenure as managing director of Megaspeed, media said. Huang Le is Alice Huang's Chinese name. Swiftdata also shares an address with Ng Wei Shi Khloe, who is listed as company secretary of both companies. Tan and Ng are the only listed officers of the two firms in their business filings. Reuters could not immediately contact Swiftdata, and Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment. Megaspeed has faced US scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to Nvidia's advanced AI chips whose export to China is restricted. On its website, it says it is an Nvidia Cloud Partner in the Asia-Pacific region and offers access to the company's GB200 NVL72 and HGX H100 systems. Megaspeed's assets increased sharply to US$3 billion in 2024 from US$33 million in 2023, its business filings showed. It reported after-tax loss of US$20 million in 2024, versus a loss of US$21,283 a year earlier, while revenue jumped to US$294 million from zero. Its cashflow statement showed US$844,555 went to investing activities in 2024, after financing activities brought in cash of US$10 million the previous year.

Related:

From affair allegations to Nvidia probe: How the Jensen Huang controversy unfolded

Who is Alice Huang, Chinese exec accused of spying on Nvidia CEO?

SINGAPORE'S ROLE Last October Singapore police said they were investigating Megaspeed over "suspected breaches of our domestic laws" after a US senator requested the Commerce Department to investigate whether Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia chips. Last month, the home affairs ministry responded to remarks in the Wall Street Journal that Singapore was concerned about Alice Huang's ties to Jensen Huang, with authorities separately investigating her alleged links to Chinese intelligence. "We would like to make clear that neither the Singapore Government nor its officials said this. And there were no such investigations conducted in respect of Alice Huang," it said, while adding that investigations into Megaspeed continue. The ministry did not immediately respond to a request for further comment on Tuesday. Singapore has become a key site for Chinese firms to set up offices in recent years, in efforts to "Singapore-wash", or domicile in the trade-focused country to reduce risks from China-US tensions. Singapore has said it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries", but it acts "firmly against companies and individuals who violate our laws and are engaged in fraudulent and dishonest practices". It is currently investigating four other individuals charged with chip fraud in an unrelated case.

Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week

Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass but conviction appears unlikely.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during an event at Sparrows Point Shipyard, in Baltimore County, Maryland, US, Oct 6, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Eric Lee)

FAST

WASHINGTON: Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, calls himself the secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. Now, with an expected House impeachment vote this week, he could soon share something in common with an actual secretary of war. William Belknap, who held that title in 1876, became the first, and to date only, civilian leader of the US military to be impeached by Congress. US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment on Monday (Nov 9), setting off a two-day clock for a potential House vote on charges including waging war against Iran without congressional approval and other abuses of power. Massie, addressing reporters, cautioned that Republican leadership could try to avoid a straight vote on impeachment by trying to dismiss it with a procedural motion.

"They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this. We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles of impeachment," he told a press conference. Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with President Donald Trump’s Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on Jan 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats. US President Donald Trump, in an interview with Reuters on Monday, strongly defended Hegseth, pointing to the US military's performance in Iran and Venezuela: "Well, he won two wars. I don't know how you can impeach him." House Speaker Mike Johnson opposed the effort, saying impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad” would be “a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see”. Voter anger over the war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections , intensifying Republican divisions over a conflict that Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned and Hegseth has defended as “courageous and historic”. Accused of taking huge kickbacks, Belknap handed President Ulysses Grant his resignation ahead of his scheduled impeachment vote and, according to a Senate history, “burst into tears”. The House impeached him anyway, but the Senate later acquitted him after falling short of the required two-thirds majority. By contrast, Hegseth is promising to stay and fight.

HEGSETH SAYS HE IS NOT WORRIED Hegseth has mounted a social media campaign, saying in a defiant video message last week that he would not back down. He also drew a comparison to Trump, who was impeached twice, saying: "It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me." Asked if he had enough Republican support to defeat the impeachment push, Hegseth said on Monday: "We're not worried about that." He announced a Tuesday press conference, his first at the Pentagon since May. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also White House national security adviser, called the impeachment push "unfair," telling reporters: "I think Pete's done a good job. I really do."

Related:

Trump, speaking with Reuters, extolled Hegseth's performance in the Iran war, which is at an impasse, and with Venezuela, where the US military deposed that country's president, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise January commando raid on his compound in the Venezuelan capital. "Well, what about impeaching the people from Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq and all of that, where we fought forever and nothing happened?" Trump asked. DEFENCE SPENDING AT RISK? Some Republican lawmakers have expressed concern that if Hegseth stays, his strained relationship with Congress will undermine the Trump administration's push for a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package. Massie, a Trump critic who is leaving office in January, warned in a statement on Monday that impeachment would be "much gentler" than what's in store for Hegseth once Democrats take control in January. "They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," Massie said. Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth over issues including the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other senior leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday he was a "hard yes" on a measure to impeach Hegseth. US Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Monday the Senate needs to put Hegseth on trial. "Hegseth waged this war illegally, in open defiance of the Constitution and multiple War Powers Resolutions this Congress passed to end the fighting," he said. Massie's articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of "high crimes and misdemeanours" ranging from waging the Iran war to various alleged abuses of power, including violating the free speech rights of US Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat. Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders. Hegseth accused them of sedition, something Trump at the time said in a social media post was "punishable by DEATH!"
